headline: Mei, “niece”, is attested in the Ryūnoshūge of 738, and its initial me- is often associated with 女 (me, “female”).
Masu, “to increase”, is simply from Old Japanese ます.
Onegai shimasu is 御 (o-) plus 願う (negau, “request, implore”) plus します, the formal form of する (suru).
Wareware is a reduplication of 我 (ware, “I; me”).
Zenkoku is Middle Chinese 全國, literally “whole country”, first attested in the mid-1800s.
Ni tsuite is に (ni, “to”) plus ついて (tsuite), the -te form of the verb 就く (tsuku).
Tsumori is the continuative stem of 積もる (tsumoru, “to intend”).
Naosu is derived from 直 (nao, “straight; common, normal, ordinary”) plus a transitive suffix, and is cognate with 治す (naosu, “to cure, to heal”).
Tairiku is an orthographic borrowing from Chinese 大陸 (dàlù).
Horu, “to dig”, is a doublet of 彫る (horu, “to carve”).
Hadagi is 肌 (hada, “skin”) plus 着 (-gi, “clothing”).
Shinshin is 心 (shin, “heart”) plus 身 (shin, “body”): the same reading twice.
Gōka is Middle Chinese 豪華, literally “grand + flowery”.
Sumi is first attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE with the phonetic spelling 須彌, and is cognate with 炭 (sumi, “charcoal”).
Kagiri is the continuative stem of 限る (kagiru, “to limit, to restrict”).
Ukagau is a doublet of 窺う (ukagau, “to peek”).
Mō has an unknown derivation; it was originally まう (mau), first attested in 1477.
Kindai is 近 (“near”) plus 代 (“age; period”).
Ou is perhaps cognate with 負う (ou, “to carry on the back”), as both involve one person moving behind another, though the accents do not match.
Ken, “ticket”, went from kwen to ken, from Middle Chinese 券 (MC khjwonH, “ticket”).
Norikaeru is 乗り (nori, “getting on, riding”) plus 換える (kaeru, “to exchange, to change”).
Sate is compared with さして (sashite, “(not) to such an extent”), and its page notes the readings さす (sasu) of kanji 扨 and 扠.
Kanai is literally “inside the house”: 家 (ka, “house”) plus 内 (nai, “inside”).
Shibō is Middle Chinese 脂肪.
Akeru, “to dawn”, is cognate with 開ける (akeru, “to open”) and 空ける (akeru, “to empty”).
Yomi is the continuative stem of 読む (yomu, “to read”).
Sode, “sleeve”, appears to be 衣 (so, “robe; clothing”) plus 手 (te, “hand; arm”), first attested in the Kojiki of 712.
Fushigi is contracted from 不可思議 (fuka shigi, literally “unfathomable”).
Muku is from Proto-Japonic *muk- (“to face”).
Bun is from Middle Chinese 分 (MC bjunH, “a minute”).
